title: Design Process
tagline: Requirements, concept generation and selection, embodiment design, design for manufacture and assembly, reliability and risk, sustainability, standards and ethics
summary: Design turns a need into a product that can be made, used safely and maintained. The course follows the design process from customer needs and specifications through concept generation and selection to embodiment and detail design, and covers design for manufacture and assembly, reliability and risk, sustainable design, standards and the professional responsibilities of engineers.
overview: Design is the part of engineering in which the problem is not fully given. A customer need, a market opportunity or a regulation has to be turned into a product that can be made, used safely, maintained and finally disposed of, and on the way the designer makes thousands of decisions with incomplete information. Analysis — the subject of most of the curriculum — predicts how a fully described artefact will behave; design proposes the artefact and uses analysis to judge it.

The course follows a product through the systematic design process of Pahl and Beitz and VDI 2221: clarifying the task and writing a measurable specification, generating concepts from a function structure, selecting among them, and developing the chosen concept into a layout and then detail documentation. Later chapters treat the qualities every design must be checked for — ease of manufacture and assembly, reliability and safety, environmental impact — and the standards, laws and professional obligations within which engineers work.

Many of the methods are simple arithmetic: present values for life-cycle cost, weighted scores, tolerance stack-ups, assembly-time estimates, reliability of series and parallel systems, life-cycle inventories. The difficulty lies elsewhere — in stating requirements that can be verified, in generating genuinely different alternatives before committing to one, in knowing what the numbers in a scoring matrix do and do not mean, and in finding the expensive mistakes early. Worked examples and case studies of real failures show where the methods help and where they mislead.

The course assumes the drawing and tolerancing of [[engineering-graphics]] and uses results from mechanics of materials and materials science where designs are sized. It is a companion to [[machine-design]], which applies the process to shafts, bearings, gears, fasteners and other machine elements.
outcomes: Describe the main models of the design process (Pahl and Beitz/VDI 2221 phases, V-model, stage-gate) and explain why they are built around iteration and early verification.
Calculate the life-cycle cost of competing designs using present values, and the expected cost of iteration and late-found defects.
Elicit customer needs and write a product specification with measurable targets and verification methods, using quality function deployment where appropriate.
Decompose a product into a function structure and generate alternative concepts with morphological charts, structured creativity methods and patent searches.
Select concepts with screening and weighted scoring matrices, test the sensitivity of the choice to the weights, and recognise dominated designs.
Develop a concept into a layout with defined architecture and interfaces, size its parts, and compute worst-case and statistical tolerance stack-ups.
Apply design-for-manufacture and design-for-assembly rules and estimate part and assembly costs to compare design alternatives.
Analyse reliability with exponential and Weibull models, reliability block diagrams, FMEA and fault trees, and reduce risk by designing hazards out.
Carry out a simple life-cycle assessment and use it to choose materials and design for disassembly, reuse and recycling.
Identify the standards and legal requirements that apply to a product, and reason about engineers' ethical responsibilities using real case studies.

chapters.title: The design process
chapters.summary: Models of the design process, design as iteration, and the engineer's role across a product's life cycle.

chapters.title: Needs and requirements
chapters.summary: Customer needs, product specifications with measurable targets, and quality function deployment.

chapters.title: Function and concept generation
chapters.summary: Functional decomposition, morphological charts, creativity methods and patents as a source of ideas.

chapters.title: Concept evaluation and selection
chapters.summary: Screening and scoring matrices, decisions under uncertainty, and early modelling of concepts.

chapters.title: Embodiment and detail design
chapters.summary: Product architecture, layout and interfaces, sizing calculations, prototyping and testing.

chapters.title: Design for manufacture and assembly
chapters.summary: Designing parts and assemblies for low cost and high quality, with rules for common processes.

chapters.title: Reliability, risk and safety
chapters.summary: Failure rates and reliability, failure modes and effects analysis, fault trees, and designing hazards out.

chapters.title: Sustainable design
chapters.summary: Life-cycle assessment, design for disassembly and recycling, and energy and material efficiency.

chapters.title: Standards, law and professional ethics
chapters.summary: Codes and standards, product liability, intellectual property and the ethical responsibilities of engineers.

history.title: First FMEA procedure
history.detail: The US military procedure MIL-P-1629, Procedures for Performing a Failure Mode, Effects and Criticality Analysis, sets out the first formal method for tracing how each component failure affects a system.

history.title: The Weibull distribution
history.detail: Waloddi Weibull publishes "A statistical distribution function of wide applicability" in the Journal of Applied Mechanics; his distribution becomes the standard model for fatigue and wear-out lives.

history.title: The first TRIZ paper
history.detail: Genrich Altshuller and Rafael Shapiro publish "On the psychology of inventive creativity" in Voprosy Psikhologii, the start of TRIZ, the theory of inventive problem solving built from patterns in patents.

history.title: Conference on Design Methods
history.detail: A conference at Imperial College London in September 1962, with proceedings edited by J. Christopher Jones and D. G. Thornley, marks the beginning of design methods as an academic field.

history.title: Pahl and Beitz's Konstruktionslehre
history.detail: Gerhard Pahl and Wolfgang Beitz publish their systematic approach to engineering design — task clarification, conceptual, embodiment and detail design; the English translation follows in 1984.

history.title: Hyatt Regency walkway collapse
history.detail: On 17 July 1981 two suspended walkways in the Kansas City Hyatt Regency fall, killing 114 people; a change from single to paired hanger rods had doubled the load on the fourth-floor connection.

history.title: Loss of Challenger
history.detail: On 28 January 1986 the O-ring seals of a solid rocket booster field joint fail in cold weather and the shuttle breaks up 73 seconds after launch, killing seven; Thiokol engineers' recommendation not to launch had been reversed.

history.title: Our Common Future
history.detail: The World Commission on Environment and Development (the Brundtland Commission) defines sustainable development as meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.

history.title: The House of Quality
history.detail: John Hauser and Don Clausing's Harvard Business Review article introduces Western engineers to quality function deployment, developed in Japan from the quality tables of Mitsubishi's Kobe shipyard (1972).

history.title: Stage-gate product development
history.detail: Robert Cooper's article in Business Horizons describes stage-gate systems, in which development stages are separated by go/kill decision points.

references.title: Engineering Design: A Systematic Approach (3rd English edition)
references.authors: Gerhard Pahl, Wolfgang Beitz, Jörg Feldhusen and Karl-Heinrich Grote
references.note: The systematic method in full: requirements lists, function structures, working principles, and the rules and principles of embodiment design.

references.title: Product Design and Development (7th edition)
references.authors: Karl T. Ulrich, Steven D. Eppinger and Maria C. Yang
references.note: Industrial practice of product development: customer needs, target specifications, concept generation and selection, product architecture, prototyping and development economics.

references.title: Engineering Design Methods: Strategies for Product Design (5th edition)
references.note: A short, readable guide to design process models and the main methods — objectives trees, function analysis, morphological charts, weighted objectives.

references.title: Engineering Design (6th edition)
references.authors: George E. Dieter and Linda C. Schmidt
references.note: A broad undergraduate text covering the process together with QFD, decision making, materials and process selection, reliability and cost evaluation.

references.title: Product Design for Manufacture and Assembly (3rd edition)
references.authors: Geoffrey Boothroyd, Peter Dewhurst and Winston Knight
references.note: The DFA method with its handling and insertion time data, and early cost estimating for the main manufacturing processes.

references.title: Practical Reliability Engineering (5th edition)
references.authors: Patrick D. T. O'Connor and Andre Kleyner
references.note: Life distributions, Weibull analysis, system reliability, FMEA, fault trees and reliability testing from an industrial viewpoint.

references.title: Materials and the Environment: Eco-informed Material Choice (3rd edition)
references.note: The eco-audit method and embodied energy and carbon data for engineering materials and processes.

references.title: Ethics in Engineering (4th edition)
references.authors: Mike W. Martin and Roland Schinzinger
references.note: Engineering as social experimentation, ethical theories, codes of conduct and the classic case studies.
